hero.title: Lab
hero.lede: Three-dimensional scaled laboratory experiments, where the deformation is produced in front of you rather than solved for.

intro: Numerical models are only as good as the physics written into them. The laboratory is where that physics is put in the way of a real material: a scaled, three-dimensional experiment deforms under its own buoyancy and viscosity, and the velocity field is measured rather than prescribed. Running the two side by side is what makes a thermo-mechanical model worth believing.

facts.label: Measurement
facts.value: Particle image velocimetry in 2-D and 3-D, with a five-axis robotic arm scanning the surface

facts.label: Forcing
facts.value: Density anomaly standing in for eclogite, and thermally dependent convection

sections.title: Three-dimensional scaled experiments
sections.body: The experiments are built in three dimensions, not as a cross-section. Lateral escape, along-strike variation and the way a structure terminates are all part of the result, and none of them survive a two-dimensional box. Each model is dynamically scaled so that the ratios governing the natural system are reproduced at laboratory size and laboratory duration: buoyancy against viscous resistance, and the timescale of deformation against the timescale of thermal diffusion.
items: Geometry, density and viscosity scaled together, so that a centimetre and an hour in the tank stand for a known distance and time in the planet.
Boundary conditions imposed on a three-dimensional volume: basal drag, lateral confinement and a free upper surface.
Repeat runs across the parameter range rather than a single illustrative experiment.

sections.title: Materials: polydimethylsiloxane and silicone oils
sections.body: The working materials are polydimethylsiloxane and a set of silicone oils. Polydimethylsiloxane behaves as a very nearly Newtonian fluid at the strain rates these experiments run at, which makes it a dependable stand-in for ductile lithosphere and for the deeper, hotter layers beneath it. Blending it, and layering it against silicone oils of different density and viscosity, builds the stratification a planet actually has.
items: Viscosity contrast between layers is the control variable: it sets whether a dense layer drips, founders coherently, or simply spreads.
Effective viscosities are measured for every batch rather than taken from a datasheet, because they shift with blend ratio, filler content and temperature.
Density contrasts are tuned with inert fillers, so buoyancy and viscosity can be varied independently.

sections.title: Starting from a density anomaly
sections.body: Most of these experiments begin compositionally rather than thermally. A layer is mixed to be denser than the fluid below it, standing in for eclogite: the dense product of a basaltic crust taken through its phase change. Left alone it is unstable, and what follows is the question — whether it drips, founders as a coherent block, or spreads without ever detaching. That outcome is set by the viscosity contrast across the interface and by how fast the dense layer can deform relative to how fast it is loaded.
items: The density contrast is tuned with inert fillers, so it can be varied without changing the viscosity alongside it.
The same setup covers drip, delamination and foundering: they are the same instability at different viscosity contrasts, not different experiments.
Surface topography is tracked throughout, because the uplift and subsidence above a founding layer is what a planet actually shows us.

sections.title: Thermally dependent, convection-driven deformation
sections.body: Where the process in question is driven by heat, the experiments are run with a thermal boundary condition rather than an imposed velocity. The material's viscosity then depends on its own temperature field, convection organises itself, and the surface deformation is a consequence of that flow instead of something applied at the edge of the box. This is the regime that matters for single-lid planets, where there is no plate boundary to impose motion.
items: Temperature-dependent viscosity, so the cold upper layer stiffens into a lid exactly as it does on a stagnant-lid planet.
Convection allowed to set its own wavelength and vigour rather than being seeded.
Deformation at the surface read as the product of the interior flow beneath it.

sections.title: Measuring the flow: particle image velocimetry
sections.body: The models are seeded with passive tracer particles and imaged through the run, and particle image velocimetry turns those image pairs into a velocity field. That is the point of the method: instead of inferring motion from the final geometry, the full field is recovered while the experiment is still running, which makes strain rate, vorticity and the partitioning of deformation directly measurable.
items: Surface and internal velocity fields recovered through the experiment, not only at its end.
Strain-rate and vorticity fields derived from the measured velocities, so localisation can be followed as it develops.
The same quantities a numerical model outputs, which is what makes the two directly comparable.

rig.name: Particle image velocimetry
rig.body: Stereo imaging of the model surface and section, from which the velocity field and the strain are computed. A five-axis robotic arm scans the surface alongside, so the topography is measured rather than inferred from the images. The high-speed camera covers events too quick to resolve at ordinary frame rates; the stereo pair carries the three-dimensional measurement.

specs.label: Stereo cameras
specs.value: LaVision, two sCMOS at 5.5 MPx, 50 Hz

sections.title: Against the thermo-mechanical models
sections.body: Each experiment is set up with a numerical counterpart in mind. The laboratory run supplies a measured velocity field under known material properties; the thermo-mechanical model is asked to reproduce it with the same scaled parameters. Where they agree, the numerical rheology is doing its job and can be pushed to planetary conditions the tank cannot reach. Where they disagree, the experiment is usually telling you something is missing from the constitutive law.
items: Measured effective viscosities and velocity fields used as the benchmark, not a qualitative resemblance of the final shape.
The same scaled parameters driving both, so a mismatch points at the physics rather than at the setup.
Results fed back into the rheology used in MILEVA and MILET.

experimentsLede: Three families of run, separated by what drives them. The first two are density-driven and ask what becomes of a layer too dense to stay where it is; the third is kinematic, and asks how shortening is taken up.

experiments.title: Lithospheric drip
experiments.body: Where the contrast is high the layer pinches into a narrow drip. The run is followed from the first perturbation through necking to detachment, which is the moment that decides whether the dense material is lost to the interior or stays hanging from the layer that made it.
items: Growth rate and final drip diameter measured against the viscosity contrast across the interface.
Detachment either completes or stalls; both outcomes are recorded, since a stalled drip is its own result.
Surface topography tracked throughout, because uplift and subsidence above the drip is what a planet shows.

figures.caption: A drip part-way down, photographed in another run.
A drip at a different viscosity contrast, as a time-lapse: the instability grows, necks and detaches.

experiments.title: Foundering across a layer
experiments.body: Lower the contrast, or let the whole layer go at once, and the behaviour changes: the dense material comes away as a coherent sheet, or as several instabilities competing for the material feeding them. In three dimensions that competition is visible; a cross-section would show one instability and miss it entirely.
items: Spacing and number of drips measured across the full layer rather than along a single section.
Drips that merge, and drips starved by a neighbour, are both ordinary outcomes here.
The same apparatus covers drip, delamination and coherent foundering: one instability at different viscosity contrasts.

figures.caption: Sheet-like foundering: the dense layer descends as a coherent curtain rather than pinching into a narrow drip. Which of the two happens is set by the viscosity contrast across the interface.
Several instabilities developing across the layer at once, with one already detached and pooled at the base of the tank.

experiments.title: Mountain building
experiments.body: Not every run is density-driven. Layered material put under progressive shortening on the deformation apparatus builds a thrust wedge, and the question becomes how that shortening is distributed: which thrusts take it up, in what order they step forward, and what the surface does above them.
items: Passive markers through the section record the internal deformation, not only the surface expression.
Thrust sequence and spacing read directly off the section as the wedge grows.
Layer strength and thickness varied between runs to change how the wedge partitions the shortening.

figures.caption: Layered analogue material under progressive shortening, building a thrust wedge. The markers scattered through the section record how the deformation is taken up inside it.

rig.name: Deformation apparatus after Hofmann
rig.body: A driven box that shortens or extends the model at a controlled rate while holding a temperature gradient across it, so that deformation and the thermal state evolve together rather than one being imposed on a fixed version of the other.
